test1_verdict.title: ±9 is NOT universal — it is axis-dependent
test1_verdict.detail: ±9 appears only in Andrews' natural layering. Transposing axes (rot1) gives ±13.5, (rot2) gives mixed irrational values (19.07, 10.07, 16.52). Unlike 2D where ±2√6 is invariant for ALL 3×3 magic squares regardless of orientation, the 3D layer eigenvalue depends on which axis you slice along. This is a fundamental 2D→3D asymmetry.
test1_verdict.implication: The Lo Shu's ±2√6 invariance is a special property of 2D: a 3×3 matrix has orientation-independent eigenvalues. In 3D, slicing along different axes produces different 3×3 matrices with different spectra. There is no single scalar 3D invariant analogous to 2√6.
test1_verdict.correction: Previous finding '±9 is the 3D spectral invariant' was too strong. Correct statement: ±9 is the layer eigenvalue of Andrews' cube in its canonical orientation.

test2_verdict.title: 4D hypercube: no clean invariant pattern
test2_verdict.detail: Valid 3×3×3×3 magic hypercube (M=123) constructed. Slice eigenvalues are messy: {30.2, 44.7, 63.6, 47.4, 27.6, 66.2} — no single value dominates. However, σ₁ = 213.042 is identical across all 3D slices, preserving first-mode isotropy.
test2_verdict.implication: The d=2 case (±2√6 universal) appears to be uniquely clean. Higher dimensions do not produce a single universal invariant. The isotropy property (identical σ₁ across modes) does generalize.

test3_verdict.title: Kronecker scaling CONFIRMED — exact at all 4 levels
test3_verdict.detail: Lo Shu Kronecker: λ_max = 15^n, λ_2 = 15^(n-1) × 2√6. Exact to machine precision at levels 1-4 (3×3 through 81×81). Full rank, zero null dimensions at every level.
test3_verdict.implication: The multiplicative eigenvalue structure of Kronecker products is algebraically guaranteed. This was expected but good to verify computationally.

test4_verdict.title: 3D query overhead: 3.73× — acceptable for production
test4_verdict.detail: 2D yantra query: 0.035ms, 3D cube query: 0.132ms (3 eigenvector projections + average). For 16,224 entities, both are sub-millisecond.
test4_verdict.implication: If 3D cube scoring adds value, the compute cost is negligible. The question is whether the extra information from 3 layer projections is semantically useful.

test5_verdict.title: Cube composite preserves ±3·2√6 but NOT the rank/null topology
test5_verdict.detail: Navagraha 2D: M=81, rank 5, null 4, λ₂=±14.697=±3·2√6. Cube composite: M=162, rank 7, null 2, λ₂=±14.697=±3·2√6. The secondary eigenvalue ±3·2√6 appears IDENTICALLY in both, despite the rank/null structure being completely different (5/4 vs 7/2).
test5_verdict.key_finding: ±3·2√6 is carried by the Lo Shu weighting, not by the cell content. Whether you fill Lo Shu positions with graha yantras or cube layers, the Lo Shu's own spectral structure imprints ±3·2√6 on the composite. The Lo Shu is the invariant carrier.
test5_verdict.implication: This confirms that the Navagraha composite's ±3·2√6 comes from the Lo Shu META-structure, not from the individual graha yantras. The yantras determine rank/null; the Lo Shu determines the invariant eigenvalue.

what_generalizes_to_3d: First-mode isotropy (σ₁ identical across all tensor modes)
Kronecker extension preserves multiplicative eigenvalue scaling
what_does_NOT_generalize: Universal scalar invariant (±2√6 is uniquely 2D — 3D eigenvalues are axis-dependent)
Composite rank/null topology (5/4 in 2D vs 7/2 in 3D composite)
overall_synthesis.surprise_finding: ±3·2√6 appearing identically in both composites proves Lo Shu is the invariant carrier. The cell content (graha yantras vs cube layers) affects topology but not the fundamental spectral constant.
